Personal history behind this paper

Overcoming a Learning Bottleneck in Impartial Games:
A Circuit Complexity Approach

Søren Riis

s.riis@qmul.ac.uk

Centre for Fundamentals of AI and Computational Theory
Queen Mary University of London
Mile End Road, London E1 4NS, United Kingdom

Abstract

Why can neural networks struggle to learn optimal play in a game with a simple, efficient solution algorithm? Motivated by empirical difficulties with parity in impartial games, we use NIM to study a representational bottleneck and three ways around it. We show that a restricted model of shallow, fixed-scale quantised networks lies in AC0\AC^0AC0, a circuit class unable to compute parity on arbitrarily large inputs. This prevents optimal single-position play across all board sizes within the model. The obstruction also guides architectural design: two-frame inputs allow restoration from a known zero-nim-sum position; complementary rollout policies reveal the missing invariant; and persistent recurrence accumulates it row by row. Each route retains shallow network components while supplying additional information or processing time. Supervised experiments illustrate the benefits of two-frame restoration and multiple rollout heads; recurrence is a theoretical construction. These results establish representational possibilities, not guarantees of successful training: AC0\AC^0AC0 does not characterise practical learnability. Core mathematical results and constructions have been checked in Lean, with classical complexity results as explicit external inputs. The interactive edition and complete Lean sources are available online (Riis, 2026a,b).

Keywords: Impartial games; NIM; circuit complexity; quantised inference; learning bottlenecks.

1 Introduction

Game play has historically served as the “Formula 1” of artificial intelligence: a high-speed, controlled proving ground where engineering limits are tested and new paradigms are born. From Deep Blue in chess to AlphaGo in Go, games have repeatedly driven advances in search, planning, and reinforcement learning (Silver et al., 2016, 2017, 2018; Schrittwieser et al., 2020). Minsky and Papert’s analysis of perceptron limitations illustrates how representational restrictions can motivate architectural changes (Minsky and Papert, 1969).

In NIM, two players take turns removing any positive number of tokens from a single heap; the player taking the last token wins. It belongs to the broad class of impartial games: both players have the same legal moves from a given position. Many such board games can be thought of as games with shared pieces, whereas in partisan games, such as chess, legal moves depend on which player is to move. NIM is central to impartial-game theory because every finite terminating impartial position under the last-move-wins convention is equivalent, in sums of games, to a single NIM heap (Section 4).

Explain this How this is formalised

NIM poses a particularly revealing challenge: optimal moves can be found by a simple, efficient algorithm, yet learning that algorithm can be difficult. The puzzle is the gap between the ease of computing the solution once the rule is known and the difficulty of discovering it through training. Friedman’s 2017 AI challenge asked whether a system could discover perfect NIM play without being given the winning strategy (Friedman, 2017a).

Our earlier work with Bei Zhou provides the empirical starting point. In Impartial Games: A Challenge for Reinforcement Learning, Zhou and Riis found that AlphaZero-style learning deteriorated as NIM boards grew (Zhou and Riis, 2026). Subsequent parity experiments examined how noisy labels can obstruct curriculum learning (Zhou and Riis, 2023); see also Zhou’s thesis (Zhou, 2024). These findings make parity a useful test of the gap between learning familiar patterns and discovering an exact rule that works across positions.

Explain this How this is formalised

Here we turn that difficulty into a question about computation. The class AC0\AC^0AC0 consists of polynomial-size Boolean circuits built from AND, OR and NOT gates, with a number of layers that remains fixed as the input grows. Such circuits can combine many local tests, but cannot compute global parity: whether the total number of input 1s is odd or even. This is the feature that makes the class useful here: it provides a precise model with a provable version of the parity limitation seen in the experiments. We establish the connection for an explicitly restricted neural model, rather than assuming that all neural networks lie in AC0\AC^0AC0.

External cited result

AC0 circuits cannot compute global parity; the connection is made for an explicitly restricted model

A published result used as background or input; not proved in Lean here.

Explain this How this is formalised

The value of identifying a bottleneck is that it tells us what an architectural change must supply. Instead of asking a shallow network to rediscover a global invariant from every board, we can expose a useful transition, obtain complementary information from rollouts, or accumulate the invariant over time. Our contribution is this barrier-to-bypass approach: a computational obstruction guides three concrete constructions. Representability in AC0\AC^0AC0 is a necessary condition for a fixed-latency computation in our restricted model; it is neither sufficient for successful training nor a universal condition on what neural networks can learn.

Informal interpretation

AC0 representability is necessary within the restricted model, not sufficient for training and not universal

Motivation, interpretation or scope; not a formal claim.

Explain this How this is formalised

NIM itself does not depend on game history: the current position completely determines its legal moves and optimal play. History can nevertheless supply useful computational context to a restricted network. The first and third bypasses use such context in different ways: an earlier board exposes a local change, while recurrent memory retains information accumulated during row processing and across positions.

Informal interpretation

History supplies computational context without changing optimal play

Motivation, interpretation or scope; not a formal claim.

Explain this How this is formalised

The central observation is that while the state can be hard to process, the transition can be easy: under the promise that the preceding position has nim-sum zero, short history converts winning-move selection into local difference computation and restoration. A second route uses distinct rollout policies to extract complementary bits of the invariant. A third route processes each position sequentially, retaining recurrent state as rows and then successive positions arrive. Here a sequence of simple updates computes the global invariant, and memory connects the new position to the preceding one. These mechanisms use different resources: explicit transition information, multiple rollout channels, or a growing recurrent computation horizon. The distinction between a shallow component and the complete computation is essential. Two-frame restoration is a shallow map on a promised pair of boards. In the other two constructions, each policy step or recurrent update is shallow, but generating the information needed for a decision takes a sequence of such steps. Thus the bypasses preserve simple network components while changing the input information or total processing time. The complete sequential computation need not itself lie in AC0\AC^0AC0. Figure 1 summarises the three routes for NIM.

1.1 Contributions

The results follow a single question: what must be added to a shallow learner to make the required strategy representable? We first identify the obstruction, then show how each bypass supplies a different missing resource.

  • AC0\AC^0AC0 containment for fixed-scale quantised inference. We formalise a fixed-grid Boolean literal-threshold model and its bounded-unrolling recurrent extension. Both are simulable by AC0\AC^0AC0 circuits (Theorem 2.4). An attention-style extension is covered only if its scoring, selection and aggregation operations can each be implemented by the permitted Boolean threshold gates. This is a restriction on the computation, not a requirement that every game have the same board size. Within a play sequence we use a fixed layout of NNN heap rows and BBB bits per heap, retaining empty heaps as zero rows. The asymptotic statements concern families of networks for growing input lengths NBNBNB.

  • Single-frame impossibility for strong mastery. Under this model, no single-frame policy/value network can strongly master NIM in the worst case (Theorem 5.2).

  • Two-frame bypass via local differences and restoration. With two consecutive frames, the agent can compute Δ(P,P′)\Delta(P,P')Δ(P,P′) in AC0\AC^0AC0 (Lemma 5.4). When PPP has nim-sum zero, an AC0\AC^0AC0 move selector restores zero after the opponent’s move (Proposition 5.5). This is conditional restoration mastery, not an arbitrary-start verifier.

  • Planning analysis and the single-policy bottleneck. We analyse a restricted measurement interface inspired by rollouts, rather than a general model of MCTS. With BBB structured policies one can recover all nim-sum bits (Proposition 5.9). Root and one-heap-modification queries to one fixed member of that family expose only one unknown linear functional (Proposition 5.10). With an explicitly bounded readout, this yields the distributional bound in Theorem 5.12.

  • Persistent recurrence via sequential row updates. A constant-depth recurrent update accumulates the nim-sum over NNN heap rows and retains a summary across position separators (Proposition 5.13). With a replay of the current board or stored heap rows, this supports optimal move selection. The construction relaxes fixed total latency, not fixed-scale quantisation (Section 5.5).

  • Controlled empirical comparison and learnability discussion. On 20-heap, 4-bit NIM with 10610^6106 supervised restoration examples, a one-frame model has low restoration accuracy while a two-frame model learns restoration (Section 7.2). In a complementary single-frame experiment, multi-head FSM-controlled shootouts achieve perfect win/loss position classification while the single-head baseline remains bottlenecked by one-bit information (Section 7.3). We also discuss why AC0\AC^0AC0 is a useful abstraction for what is robustly feasible under fixed-scale quantised inference (Section 6.3).

1.2 Scope and limitations

Our theorems are worst-case representational statements about what can be computed under explicit architectural constraints. They are not training-complexity results, and they intentionally abstract away from several practical details, such as continuous-valued activations, floating-point arithmetic, normalisation layers and the dynamics of optimisation.

  • Fixed-scale quantisation / fixed latency. The AC0\AC^0AC0 simulation (Theorem 2.4) assumes constant depth and a fixed-scale, bounded-range quantisation regime: weights/thresholds lie on a fixed grid whose range/resolution do not scale with the input length (cf. Remark 2.2). Architectures that rely on fan-in dependent re-normalisation, biases/thresholds growing with dimension, or depth growing with nnn fall outside this abstraction. In particular, a fixed recurrent update rule need not have fixed total latency: the third bypass deliberately allows NNN successive row updates per position.

  • Formal model vs. experimental networks. The formal units have nonnegative weights on Boolean literals and bounded thresholds. The experiments instead use ordinary floating-point signed linear layers, ReLU and LayerNorm, with Log-Softmax in the loss. They test the benefit of transition information under the reported training protocol, not the asymptotic lower bound or the deployment behaviour of quantised networks.

  • Stylised planning interface. The single-channel lower bound permits only root and one-heap-modification queries to a fixed structured policy, and requires a polynomial-size, constant-depth final readout. It is not a bound on arbitrary rollout policies, unrestricted query transformations, or an unbounded adaptive MCTS controller.

  • No guarantee of learnability. The multi-policy-head and recurrent constructions concern existence of suitable computations; we do not claim that self-play efficiently discovers the structured heads or an exact recurrent accumulator. Our experiments use controlled supervised restoration and policy imitation; self-play discovery is left for a separate study.

1.3 Paper organisation

Section 2 introduces the fixed-scale quantised inference model and the AC0\AC^0AC0 simulation theorem. Section 3 situates our contribution in circuit complexity, modern sequence models, and reinforcement learning for combinatorial games. Section 4 recalls NIM and the nim-sum characterisation. Section 5 presents the main impossibility and bypass results: two-frame restoration, rollout channels (Section 5.4), and persistent recurrence (Section 5.5). Section 6 discusses modelling choices and learnability considerations. Section 7 reports experiments. Appendices contain formal model definitions and proofs.

2 Theoretical framework and neural network models

2.1 Fixed-scale quantised inference and AC0\AC^0AC0 simulation

We consider neural inference models that are (i) bounded depth, (ii) polynomial size, and (iii) operate in a fixed-scale quantised regime: all weights and thresholds lie on a fixed quantisation grid of bounded dynamic range that does not change with the input length. The fixed scale is motivated by limits on the effective precision of neural computation, including sensitivity to noise: distinctions that can be used reliably may be much coarser than the rounding resolution of 32-bit floating-point arithmetic. Noise motivates this abstraction; it does not by itself imply the gate and threshold assumptions below.

Our Boolean threshold gates sum nonnegative weights on inputs that may be negated. Negation allows inhibitory as well as excitatory effects: for a Boolean input xxx, the identity −ax=a(1−x)−a-ax=a(1-x)-a−ax=a(1−x)−a replaces a negative coefficient by a positive weight on the negated input, with an adjustment to the threshold. The substantive restriction is that the resulting weights and thresholds remain on the fixed, bounded grid; this is not a model of arbitrary signed-weight or INT8/fixed-point inference.

Concretely, we fix constants:

  • a quantisation resolution parameter captured by a fixed denominator D∈ND\in\ND∈N (grid step 1/D1/D1/D),

  • a dynamic-range bound W∈NW\in\NW∈N (maximum magnitude W/DW/DW/D),

  • and (for recurrent/attention models) a finite time window T∈NT\in\NT∈N.

We define QW,D  =  {ℓD : ℓ∈{0,1,2,…,W}},\Qset_{W,D} \;=\; \Big\{ \frac{\ell}{D}\ :\ \ell\in\{0,1,2,\dots,W\}\Big\},QW,D​={Dℓ​ : ℓ∈{0,1,2,…,W}}, a finite set independent of input length. The threshold bound applies after choosing the literal representation. Replacing a signed term −ax-a x−ax by a(1−x)a(1-x)a(1−x) raises the threshold by aaa. With many such terms, the adjusted threshold may grow with the input length. What matters is the amount of evidence needed to activate a gate: our model bounds the number of satisfied input literals that suffice, whereas an unrestricted majority gate needs a number that grows with its inputs. Negative coefficients themselves are not the obstruction; the bound on the adjusted threshold is essential to the simulation.

Why fixed-scale quantisation suggests an AC0\AC^0AC0 abstraction. The key structural property is fixed scale: the smallest nonzero weight is 1/D1/D1/D and the largest threshold is W/DW/DW/D, with W,DW,DW,D independent of the input length. Consequently, whenever a threshold unit outputs 111, there is a satisfying witness consisting of at most WWW input literals whose contributions already cross the threshold. This yields a constant-width DNF expansion for each unit (Lemma B.1), and composing a constant number of layers yields an AC0\AC^0AC0 simulation (Theorem 2.4).

We emphasise that this is not a statement about floating-point arithmetic per se. The abstraction intentionally excludes scale-adaptive regimes where thresholds/biases grow with fan-in or where weights shrink with dimension (e.g. 1/n1/n1/n or 1/n1/\sqrt{n}1/n​ normalisations), which move the analysis toward threshold-circuit classes such as TC0\TC^0TC0. This class allows constant-depth, polynomial-size circuits with general threshold gates, including majority gates; unlike AC0\AC^0AC0, it can compute parity.

Remark 2.2 (Scope of the AC0\AC^0AC0 abstraction) Theorem 2.4 formalises a fixed-latency fixed-scale quantised regime in which each unit uses parameters drawn from a bounded-range grid QW,D\Qset_{W,D}QW,D​ with W,DW,DW,D independent of the input length. This yields the constant-witness property exploited in Lemma B.1.

The abstraction is deliberately conservative: it does not model architectures that rely on fan-in dependent re-scaling, numerically large signed biases/thresholds that grow with dimension, or deep computations whose depth scales with nnn. Allowing such scale-adaptive behaviour leads naturally to richer threshold-circuit models (e.g. TC0\TC^0TC0), in which parity-like computations can become representable.

Remark 2.3 (Local vs. global parity) When we say “parity is hard” we mean global parity across the full Boolean input of length n=NBn=NBn=NB. In contrast, parity on O(1)O(1)O(1) bits is trivial in AC0\AC^0AC0 (hardwire the truth table), and more generally XOR of a constant number of BBB-bit blocks is AC0\AC^0AC0-computable. This local/global separation underlies both the two-frame bypass via the nimber difference Δ(P,P′)\Delta(P,P')Δ(P,P′) and the recurrent bypass, which composes local XOR updates over a growing number of steps.

Notation convention (input length). We write NNN for the number of heaps and BBB (or kkk in experiments) for the bit-width used to encode each heap size. The resulting Boolean input length is n:=NBn := NBn:=NB. When we discuss AC0\AC^0AC0 circuit size/depth, nnn always refers to this Boolean input length.

Circuit complexity primer. AC0\AC^0AC0 is the class of Boolean functions computable by constant-depth, polynomial-size circuits with unbounded fan-in AND/OR/NOT gates. A classical result is that PARITY∉AC0\mathrm{PARITY}\notin\AC^0PARITY∈/AC0. In contrast, TC0\TC^0TC0 augments AC0\AC^0AC0 with unbounded fan-in threshold gates and can compute parity. Our focus here is a fixed-scale quantised regime in which thresholds do not scale with fan-in; in that regime, each threshold unit admits a constant-witness DNF expansion and the overall computation collapses to AC0\AC^0AC0 (Theorem 2.4).

2.2 Simulation by circuits

We state the simulation theorem for the literal-threshold model and its explicitly gate-realised extensions.

Theorem 2.4 (Simulation by AC0\AC^0AC0) Fix constants W,D∈NW,D\in\NW,D∈N and a time window T∈NT\in\NT∈N. Let {Mn}n≥1\{\mathcal{M}_n\}_{n\ge 1}{Mn​}n≥1​ be any family of models of type NN\NNNN, RNN\RNNRNN (with window TTT), or LTST\LTSTLTST (with window TTT) such that:

  1. (1) (Polynomial size) the number of neurons/units in Mn\mathcal{M}_nMn​ is at most poly(n)\poly(n)poly(n).

  2. (2) (Constant depth) the number of layers is a fixed constant LLL (independent of nnn); for RNN/LTST\RNN/\LTSTRNN/LTST the entire unrolled computation uses at most TTT time steps from an input-independent initial state.

  3. (3) (Permitted primitives) every operation is realised by the Boolean literal-threshold gates of Definition A.1; all weights and thresholds lie in QW,D\Qset_{W,D}QW,D​. For the attention-style extension this includes score computation, coefficient selection and aggregation.

Then the Boolean function computed by Mn\mathcal{M}_nMn​ can be computed by an AC0\AC^0AC0 circuit family of polynomial size and constant depth (depending only on L,T,W,DL,T,W,DL,T,W,D).

3 Related Work

Circuit complexity and neural networks. Parity is outside AC0\AC^0AC0 (Furst et al., 1984; Håstad, 1986), while constant-depth threshold circuits (TC0\TC^0TC0) can compute it. Attention results depend on the precise model: Hao, Angluin and Frank analyse hard-attention variants, including AC0\AC^0AC0 restrictions for unique hard attention (Hao et al., 2022). Merrill and Sabharwal study the additional power of intermediate decoding over a TC0\TC^0TC0 baseline (Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024); that containment does not rule out parity. Their sequential-computation perspective is relevant to our recurrent bypass, although the architectures and formal assumptions differ. Our contribution applies these distinctions to NIM policies and a restricted rollout-measurement interface.

Quantised inference and deployment constraints. Low-bit inference motivates studying bounded numerical resources (Jacob et al., 2018; Dettmers et al., 2022). Our constant-witness proof additionally requires nonnegative literal weights, bounded thresholds and Boolean intermediate states. These are explicit mathematical assumptions, not properties inferred merely from a quantisation format. Standard signed linear layers and scale-adaptive normalisation are outside the theorem unless separately reduced to the permitted gates.

Reinforcement learning in combinatorial games. While RL has mastered domains such as Go and chess, impartial games remain a useful stress test because optimality is governed by exact algebraic invariants rather than approximate pattern matching. Zhou and Riis (Zhou and Riis, 2026, 2023) studied reinforcement-learning difficulties in impartial games. Our lower bound identifies a representational obstruction in a restricted model; determining which mechanisms explain failures in ordinary neural training requires separate experiments.

External cited result

Prior work on RL difficulties in impartial games; the lower bound is about a restricted model

A published result used as background or input; not proved in Lean here.

Explain this How this is formalised

History and memory in RL. Using short history windows is standard in partially observable settings, where stacked frames recover hidden variables such as velocity (Mnih et al., 2015). Our point is different and perhaps surprising: even in Markovian, fully observable games—where the current state is informationally sufficient and the past is theoretically irrelevant—history can reduce computational complexity by exposing local differences that would otherwise require expensive search or unbounded-depth inference to extract from the current state alone. In our restoration setting, the previous frame carries a promise established by an earlier successful move: its nim-sum is zero. That promise makes a local difference sufficient for the next response. Establishing the promise initially remains a separate computational task.

Informal interpretation

History can reduce computational complexity even in fully observable games, given the zero-nim-sum promise

4 Impartial games and NIM

We briefly recall standard definitions; see (Berlekamp et al., 2001–2004) for extensive background.

4.1 Impartial games

Definition 4.1 (Impartial game) A finite terminating impartial game is a pair (P,M)(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{M})(P,M) where P\mathcal{P}P is a nonempty set of positions and M(p)⊆P\mathcal{M}(p)\subseteq \mathcal{P}M(p)⊆P is the (finite) set of legal moves from ppp, with the property that the move relation does not depend on which player is to play (symmetry). We assume the move relation is acyclic and play terminates. We use the last-move-wins convention, usually called normal play: a player with no legal move loses.

The last-move-wins convention also provides a convenient encoding of other decisive endings. A move that wins by capturing a designated piece or creating a specified configuration can simply lead to a position with no further legal moves. If instead reaching a special position loses for the player who made the move, give the opponent one forced move to a new terminal position. These encodings preserve the winner of the individual play; they must retain player-independent move rules to remain impartial. The theory below concerns the resulting normal-play game.

4.3 Sprague–Grundy theory and nim-sum

The breadth of impartial games makes the Sprague–Grundy theorem remarkable: every finite terminating impartial position under normal play is equivalent to a single NIM heap of some size, called its nimber or Grundy value. Equivalence here means that replacing the position by that heap preserves the winning or losing status of its sum with any other such game. In a disjunctive sum, a move is made in exactly one component. The nimber of a sum is the bitwise XOR of the component nimbers; in particular, the nimber of a NIM board is the XOR of its heap sizes.

Why NIM is a useful barrier example. For a disjunctive sum of independent impartial components, the Grundy value is the XOR of the component nimbers. If these nimbers can vary independently so that their aggregation contains an unbounded parity subproblem, NIM isolates the resulting aggregation obstruction. Learning NIM would therefore address a fundamental component of impartial-game play, but would not by itself solve self-play learning for the wider class: determining component nimbers can be computationally difficult (Section 8.3). Nor does every impartial game contain a hard parity aggregation task. Our unconditional lower bound concerns NIM; extensions require an explicit encoding and reduction.

Informal interpretation

NIM isolates the XOR aggregation obstruction; extensions to other games need explicit reductions

5 Main results: impossibility and possibility

We first establish the single-frame barrier under fixed total latency, then develop three bypasses: recent-history inputs, multiple rollout channels, and persistent row-wise recurrence.

5.1 Mastery notions

We distinguish three notions of mastery:

Definition 5.1 (Strong, weak, and restoration mastery) An agent achieves strong mastery of NIM if it chooses a winning move at every NNN-position where it is to move, including positions reached by arbitrary legal play by both players. Reachability is relative to the specified initial positions and player role; unrestricted strong mastery allows every initial position.

It achieves weak mastery relative to an initial position p0p_0p0​ and a designated player role if, whenever that role has a winning strategy from p0p_0p0​, its own strategy wins against every opponent strategy. The guarantee concerns histories consistent with its own preceding actions, not every position reachable under arbitrary actions by both players. For asymptotic claims, the initial positions form a specified family. Strategies may depend on the complete history. Opponent moves are legal; a missing or illegal agent move counts as a loss. On an initially losing position the weak-mastery condition imposes no requirement.

It achieves restoration mastery if, whenever the opponent moves from a PPP-position QQQ with nim⁡(Q)=0\operatorname{nim}(Q)=0nim(Q)=0 to a position Q′Q'Q′, the agent responds with a move Q′→RQ'\to RQ′→R such that nim⁡(R)=0\operatorname{nim}(R)=0nim(R)=0.

We use standard impartial-game terminology: a PPP-position is losing for the player to move, and an NNN-position is winning. For NIM, Theorem 4.4 says that PPP-positions are exactly the positions with nim-sum 000. Equivalently, weak mastery requires the agent to move to a PPP-position at every one of its decision histories consistent with its own earlier actions, starting from an initial position winnable in its designated role. This distinction allows a simple strategy to master a family without solving positions it never encounters under its own play; Appendix D gives examples.

5.2 Single-frame impossibility results

In a single-frame representation, the network sees only the current position. To play optimally, it must in effect determine whether the nim-sum is zero and, if not, find a move producing nim-sum zero. The core obstacle is that global nim-sum computation requires parity-like behaviour across many bits, and parity is not in AC0\AC^0AC0 (Furst et al., 1984; Håstad, 1986; Smolensky, 1987; Razborov, 1987).

Theorem 5.2 (Single-frame parity barrier) Consider the restricted family of NIM positions P(b)=(2,b1,…,bm)P(\mathbf{b})=(2,b_1,\dots,b_m)P(b)=(2,b1​,…,bm​) where bi∈{0,1}b_i\in\{0,1\}bi​∈{0,1}. Any single-frame agent that achieves strong mastery must compute the parity b1⊕⋯⊕bmb_1\oplus\cdots\oplus b_mb1​⊕⋯⊕bm​. Since PARITY∉AC0\mathrm{PARITY}\notin \AC^0PARITY∈/AC0, no polynomial-size, constant-depth fixed-scale quantised network can strongly master NIM.

Proof. Since each bi∈{0,1}b_i\in\{0,1\}bi​∈{0,1}, these positions have nimber 2⊕(b1⊕⋯⊕bm)2\oplus(b_1\oplus\cdots\oplus b_m)2⊕(b1​⊕⋯⊕bm​), which is either 222 or 333. A winning move must change the first heap: changing any other heap leaves the leading binary digit of the nim-sum unchanged. To obtain nimber zero, the first heap must be reduced to b1⊕⋯⊕bmb_1\oplus\cdots\oplus b_mb1​⊕⋯⊕bm​. Thus the unique winning move removes two tokens when this parity is zero and one when it is one. Encoding each heap in two bits uses only constants and wiring, and the low bit of the replacement heap is the input parity. This gives a constant-depth, polynomial-size reduction to winning-move selection, although every encoded position is winning.□

5.3 First bypass: two-frame restoration

The fundamental idea is to avoid computing the global nim-sum from scratch. Instead, we exploit that each move changes only one heap, so the nimber difference between consecutive positions is locally computable.

5.4 Second bypass: structured rollout policies

Theorem 5.2 shows that no AC0\AC^0AC0 circuit can evaluate the nim-sum in a single forward pass. A natural follow-up is whether planning—testing candidate moves and simulating play, as in Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)—can compensate.

We analyse a stylised rollout interface: a planning algorithm queries a rollout policy π\piπ by simulating a complete game in which both players follow π\piπ from a start position, and it observes only the terminal win/loss bit. This abstraction isolates the information that a weak policy can expose through repeated simulation; it is not a claim about the optimisation dynamics of AlphaZero-style training (cf. Section 1.2).

Definition 5.6 (Rollout policy and rollout outcome) A deterministic rollout policy maps a nonterminal NBNBNB-bit NIM position to a legal move, encoded by a heap index and its new value; on the terminal position it outputs a halt symbol. It is AC0\AC^0AC0-bounded when this map has polynomial-size, constant-depth circuits. A rollout has both players follow that policy until termination. Its outcome ROπ(P)\mathrm{RO}_{\pi}(P)ROπ​(P) is 1 if the first player wins and 0 otherwise, including at a terminal start. The interface returns only this terminal bit, not a trajectory or move count.

The finite-state shootout controller introduced above is the natural generalisation of this idea: it does not change what any head can compute, but organises the heads into an adaptive querying protocol—the controller decides which channel to query next (and when to stop, or when to re-query for robustness) based on previously observed rollout outcomes. In this view, multi-head provides the channels, while the FSM provides the sequential control that turns those channels into a practical evaluation procedure.

5.5 Third bypass: persistent row-wise recurrence

The two-frame construction supplies the relevant history explicitly, while the multi-head construction obtains additional information through complete rollouts. A third possibility is to let the agent build and retain its own state by processing the board sequentially. The recurrent update remains simple, but the number of updates is allowed to grow with the input. The construction uses the elementary running-XOR algorithm. In correspondence reproduced by Friedman (Friedman, 2017b), John Schulman proposed feeding NIM heaps one at a time to a recurrent network and reported preliminary supervised nim-sum experiments. Here we make the shallow updates, separator and state protocols, and move-selection constructions explicit, distinguishing their representational guarantees from learning through self-play.

Serialising positions and retaining state. Write position Pt=(xt,1,…,xt,N)P_t=(x_{t,1},\ldots,x_{t,N})Pt​=(xt,1​,…,xt,N​), with each heap represented by one BBB-bit row. Feed successive positions as the stream x1,1,…,x1,N⏟P1, SEP,x2,1,…,x2,N⏟P2, SEP,….\underbrace{x_{1,1},\ldots,x_{1,N}}_{P_1},\ \mathtt{SEP},\quad \underbrace{x_{2,1},\ldots,x_{2,N}}_{P_2},\ \mathtt{SEP},\quad\ldots .P1​x1,1​,…,x1,N​​​, SEP,P2​x2,1​,…,x2,N​​​, SEP,…. Each row arrives as a block of BBB bits together with a row/separator tag. A separator marks the end of a complete position; the agent chooses a move only after that position has been read. The next observed position is then appended to the stream. For comparisons of individual heaps, indices remain aligned across positions, including rows for empty heaps. A scan of the current board suffices for nim-sum evaluation without earlier game positions; cross-position memory additionally supports the comparisons below. The hidden state is carried across rows and position boundaries. A separator resets the accumulator for the next scan while preserving selected information about the completed position; it does not reset the entire memory.

A one-step recurrent dependency can nevertheless carry information accumulated over the whole stream. The bypass comes from sequential computation with retained state, not from the delimiter itself. For growing heap bit-width, the accumulator also needs O(B)O(B)O(B) bits; a fixed-width hidden state is not claimed to store arbitrary-size invariants or histories. The construction establishes representational sufficiency for NIM, but does not establish that training a recurrent network will discover the update or preserve it reliably over long games. 5.6 What the three bypasses establish

Proposition 5.14 (Shallow components and complete strategies) For N≥1N\ge1N≥1 heaps of B≥1B\ge1B≥1 bits, the following constructions use polynomial-size, constant-depth Boolean components, realisable by literal-threshold networks with weights and thresholds in {0,1}\{0,1\}{0,1}.

  1. (i) The two-frame selector maps a legal transition Q→Q′Q\to Q'Q→Q′ from nim⁡(Q)=0\operatorname{nim}(Q)=0nim(Q)=0 to a legal binary-encoded response restoring zero. Retaining the response board as the next predecessor gives a winning strategy from this established invariant, with the opponent to move.

  2. (ii) Each structured rollout policy and the readout from the board and its BBB outcome bits are shallow. Executing the rollouts and then the readout gives a winning strategy from any nonzero nim-sum board, using at most BN(2B−1)BN(2^B-1)BN(2B−1) simulated game moves per decision.

  3. (iii) The recurrent state update is shallow. Iterating it over the replay protocol gives a winning strategy from any nonzero nim-sum board, with O(B+log⁡N)O(B+\log N)O(B+logN) memory and 2N+22N+22N+2 updates per decision.

Here “winning strategy” quantifies over every legal opponent response. Polynomial size and constant depth refer to the indicated component, with depth independent of NNN and BBB; they do not bound the number of sequential component evaluations.

Proof outline. Appendix C gives explicit candidate tests, first-index encoding and a fixed-scale implementation. The two-frame circuit computes the changed heap’s XOR difference, which equals the current nim-sum under the stated promise. The multi-head readout reconstructs that same invariant from the executed rollout outcomes. The recurrent controller obtains it by accumulation and uses the stored result during replay. In each case the selected move restores zero; every legal opponent move makes the nim-sum nonzero, and every move decreases the total number of stones. This proves termination and the winning guarantee. For the two-frame strategy, the newly restored board is precisely the frame retained for the next response. For recurrence, the finite controller state persists between decisions. The rollout and recurrent step bounds are those proved above.□

These are three ways around the same restricted inference problem, not three shallow algorithms for unrestricted parity. The two-frame construction changes the input and imposes a promise. The other constructions allow processing time to grow. Their complete board-to-winning-move maps cannot themselves form an AC0\AC^0AC0 family: otherwise applying either to (2,b1,…,bm)(2,b_1,\ldots,b_m)(2,b1​,…,bm​) would contradict Theorem 5.2. Parallel output heads alone do not supply the rollout computation, and separators alone do not supply a recurrent scan. Appendix C illustrates the explicit network constructions and explains their conservative depth and layer bounds.

6 Learning impartial games with neural networks

The results above are primarily representational: they identify what information a bounded-depth, fixed-scale quantised model can or cannot compute from its input, and how history, multiple rollout heads, or a growing recurrent horizon can supply the missing information. This section connects the theory to the training protocols used in Section 7 and highlights the main modelling choice (AC0\AC^0AC0 vs. TC0\TC^0TC0).

6.1 Practical takeaways

  • Single-frame is brittle to parity. In the worst case, fixed-scale quantised bounded-depth inference cannot reliably represent the nim-sum or a winning move selector (Section 5.2).

  • Three bypasses with different resources. A two-frame input exposes the transition signal Δ(P,P′)\Delta(P,P')Δ(P,P′) and supports restoration (Section 5.3.1); multiple rollout heads recover the missing nim-sum bits through depth amplification (Section 5.4); persistent recurrence accumulates the invariant over sequential row updates and retains summaries across positions (Section 5.5). The last route trades fixed total latency for a growing processing horizon.

  • Optimisation remains nontrivial. Even when a solution is expressible in AC0\AC^0AC0, discovering it from sparse win/loss rewards can be difficult; our experiments therefore isolate a dense restoration supervision signal and separately report rollout-based classification.

6.3 Approximate majority, parity, and the AC0\AC^0AC0 abstraction

One might object that modern networks can implement majority-like decisions, suggesting TC0\TC^0TC0 (threshold circuits) as the “right” complexity class. Indeed, if one allows scale-adaptive thresholds/biases or fan-in dependent re-scaling, constant-depth threshold models can represent parity-type computations.

External cited result

Scale-adaptive threshold models (TC0) can represent parity

A published result used as background or input; not proved in Lean here.

Explain this How this is formalised

Our focus is a restricted literal-threshold regime: fixed total depth, nonnegative weights on Boolean literals, and thresholds bounded in units of the smallest nonzero weight. In this regime, each gate has a constant-size witness and collapses to a constant-width DNF, yielding an AC0\AC^0AC0 abstraction (Theorem 2.4). Constant-depth AC0\AC^0AC0 circuits can implement approximate counting (Ajtai, 1993), yet they have exponentially small correlation with parity (Furst et al., 1984; Håstad, 1986; Smolensky, 1987; Razborov, 1987). Learning parity depends on the architecture and training setting; both difficulties and positive results have been studied (Thornton, 1996b,a; Daniely and Malach, 2020). The representational lower bound here applies only to the explicit gate model. Section 6.4 gives a complementary Fourier/spectral interpretation of this local-versus-global parity separation.

External cited result

In the restricted regime gates collapse to AC0; AC0 approximates counting but has tiny parity correlation

AC0\AC^0AC0 has little high-frequency mass. A seminal theorem of Linial–Mansour–Nisan shows that AC0\AC^0AC0 functions have almost all Fourier mass on low degrees: for fff computed by an ACd0\AC^0_dACd0​ circuit of size MMM, the tail above degree kkk decays rapidly with kkk (see (Linial et al., 1993), and sharper bounds in (Tal, 2015)). For fixed depth and polynomial size, correlation with full parity under the uniform distribution is negligible in nnn. Applying this statement to other subsets requires specifying their size relative to circuit depth and size, and it does not automatically apply under a nonuniform training distribution.

Local vs. global parity in NIM. In our encoding, the jjjth bit of the nim-sum is the parity of the jjjth bits across all NNN heaps, hence a degree-NNN character. Conditional on a specified changed heap iii, the sign encoding of the jjjth delta bit is the two-coordinate character (−1)xi,j+xi,j′(-1)^{x_{i,j}+x'_{i,j}}(−1)xi,j​+xi,j′​. When the changed index is unknown, the delta bit is specified on pairs of boards differing in at most one heap. A shallow extension to all pairs is dj(P,P′)=⋁i=1N(xi,j⊕xi,j′).d_j(P,P')=\bigvee_{i=1}^{N}(x_{i,j}\oplus x'_{i,j}).dj​(P,P′)=i=1⋁N​(xi,j​⊕xi,j′​).(6.2) On the promised domain this is the required delta bit. For N≥2N\ge2N≥2, its sign encoding (−1)dj(-1)^{d_j}(−1)dj​ is not a single character, even up to sign; for N=1N=1N=1 it is exactly a degree-two character. Thus local computability does not mean that the full unknown-index map has degree two. It follows from the explicit AC0\AC^0AC0 construction in Lemma 5.4.

Fourier degree also aligns with a common empirical observation in deep learning: gradient-based training tends to fit low-frequency components before high-frequency ones (“spectral bias” / “frequency principle”) (Rahaman et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2019). This suggests a possible analogy for parity learning, but continuous-domain spectral-bias observations do not prove how SGD learns Boolean parity or restoration under our nonuniform data distribution. The core representational point is that the global invariant nim⁡(P)\operatorname{nim}(P)nim(P) is hard to compute from a single frame, whereas the transition quantity Δ(P,P′)\Delta(P,P')Δ(P,P′) is locally computable from two frames (Lemma 5.4). 7 Experiments

The stronger experimental goal would be to show that an AlphaZero-style learner discovers effective play through self-play once a bypass is available. We do not establish that here. The theoretical barrier concerns what the restricted network can represent, independently of training; removing it leaves open whether the required computation can be learned, with what data and under which training regime.

Informal interpretation

The experiments do not show that an AlphaZero-style learner discovers the bypasses by self-play

Motivation, interpretation or scope; not a formal claim.

Explain this How this is formalised

We take a controlled intermediate step: supervised restoration learning from teacher–random transitions (Section 7.2) and a complementary single-frame multi-head shootout evaluation with imitated policy heads (Section 7.3). These experiments supply guidance that outcome-only self-play would have to generate for itself. They test whether the proposed information and computation can be useful in training, while also exposing difficulties that remain after the input has been enriched. Unless otherwise stated, both one-frame (1F) and two-frame (2F) agents share the same action parameterisation and network architecture (Section 7.1).

7.1 Neural architecture and training objective

7.1.1 State and action representation

We use a fixed-width binary encoding of heap sizes with kkk bits per heap. The single-frame input is the encoding of the current heap vector. The two-frame input concatenates the encodings of the previous and current heap vectors. When a previous frame is unavailable (e.g. on the first move of a game), we set the previous frame equal to the current position so that the input dimension is constant and the 2F policy remains well-defined.

The action space is parameterised as “set heap iii to value vvv” for i∈{1,…,N}i\in\{1,\dots,N\}i∈{1,…,N} and v∈{0,1,…,2k−1}v\in\{0,1,\dots,2^k-1\}v∈{0,1,…,2k−1}, giving N⋅2kN\cdot 2^kN⋅2k logits. The saved restoration evaluation takes an unmasked argmax over all logits; illegal predictions count as incorrect. Legality masking is used in the separate game-playing and FSM rollout routines. These are distinct evaluation conventions.

7.1.2 Network architecture

Both restoration agents use a policy-only MLP with two hidden layers and N⋅2kN\cdot2^kN⋅2k output logits. There is no value head in the saved implementation. The two-frame input has dimension 2Nk2Nk2Nk; the single-frame input has dimension NkNkNk. The template and hidden width are shared, but parameter counts differ: the two-frame first layer adds NkH=20,480NkH=20{,}480NkH=20,480 parameters in the reported setting. All layers use ordinary floating-point arithmetic; these networks are not literal implementations of the FSQI gate model.

7.1.3 Training targets and loss

For each training input (single-frame state or two-frame state-pair), the target is a soft distribution πopt(⋅∣p′)\pi_{\mathrm{opt}}(\cdot\mid p')πopt​(⋅∣p′) over optimal restoration moves. The policy head is trained with cross-entropy to this target. The soft-target cross-entropy also uses unmasked logits. No value loss is used in this supervised restoration experiment.

7.1.4 Evaluation criteria in this version

In this version we report two task-level notions of performance rather than full game-level Elo tournaments. Move-level restoration performance is measured by functional correctness: on a test position with nonzero nim-sum, a move is counted as correct if it produces a successor state with nim-sum zero. Positions with zero nim-sum have no winning move (Theorem 4.4); when reporting functional correctness we therefore condition on nonzero nim-sum positions. Position-level evaluation performance is measured by P/NP/NP/N classification accuracy and NNN-position recall in FSM-controlled shootouts (Section 7.3).

7.2 Supervised restoration learning from teacher–random transitions

This experiment isolates the restoration response as a supervised learning problem. In normal-play impartial games, a restoration response is the move that returns play to a losing (PPP-)position after the opponent departs from it. In Nim, this is equivalent to selecting an optimal (winning) move from the post-opponent position: if the previous position had nim-sum 000, then after any opponent move the position is winning, and any optimal reply restores nim-sum 000.

Checked theorem

After any move from a zero-nim-sum position, every optimal reply restores nim-sum zero

Explain this How this is formalised Lean statement and source

Motivated by Sections 5.2–5.3, the experiment asks a separate empirical question under a fixed supervised training protocol: does access to the transition (p,p′)(p,p')(p,p′) (two frames) enable successful restoration learning under this protocol, even when the one-frame model fails? This benchmark builds on the observation that parity-type invariants pose a challenge for reinforcement learning in impartial games (Zhou and Riis, 2026, 2023), while explicitly providing the transition information needed by Proposition 5.5.

7.2.1 Game and representations

We consider Nim with N=20N=20N=20 heaps. Each heap size is represented with k=4k=4k=4 bits (little-endian), so heap values lie in {0,…,15}\{0,\ldots,15\}{0,…,15}. Moves are represented in a fixed action space of size N⋅2k=20⋅16=320N\cdot 2^k = 20\cdot 16 = 320N⋅2k=20⋅16=320: an action chooses a heap index iii and a new heap value vvv. Legality requires 0≤v<hi0\le v<h_i0≤v<hi​; the reported unmasked metric counts violations as errors.

A 1-frame (1F) policy receives only the current position p′p'p′ (80-bit input), while a 2-frame (2F) policy receives the concatenation (p,p′)(p,p')(p,p′) of the previous and current positions (160-bit input). Both agents use the shared MLP architecture described in Section 7.1 (two hidden layers of width H=256H=256H=256).

7.2.2 Dataset generation (teacher–random–teacher)

We generate a dataset of size D=106D=10^6D=106 examples of the form (p,p′)↦πopt(⋅∣p′),(p, p') \mapsto \pi_{\mathrm{opt}}(\cdot \mid p') ,(p,p′)↦πopt​(⋅∣p′), where πopt(⋅∣p′)\pi_{\mathrm{opt}}(\cdot \mid p')πopt​(⋅∣p′) is a soft target distribution over optimal moves from p′p'p′.

Empirical result

Teacher–random–teacher dataset of 10⁶ examples with soft optimal-move labels

Supported by saved experimental runs, not by a proof.

Explain this How this is formalised

Each example is generated as follows:

  1. 1. Sample a random winning Nim position sss (nim-sum ≠0\ne 0=0).

  2. 2. Apply an optimal teacher move from sss to obtain ppp. For optimal play in Nim, ppp has nim-sum 000 (a PPP-position for the next player).

  3. 3. Apply a uniformly random legal move from ppp to obtain p′p'p′.

  4. 4. Define the label πopt(⋅∣p′)\pi_{\mathrm{opt}}(\cdot \mid p')πopt​(⋅∣p′) as the uniform distribution over all optimal (winning) moves from p′p'p′.

This construction ensures that each training input (p,p′)(p,p')(p,p′) corresponds to the canonical restoration setting: ppp is a PPP-position, the random move produces a winning position p′p'p′, and the label is the set of restoration moves back to a PPP-position.

Why teacher–random–teacher? We do not sample arbitrary triples (P,P′,a)(P,P',a)(P,P′,a) uniformly at random, because the restoration claim is about a specific interaction regime: the opponent departs a PPP-position and the agent must restore it. The teacher step ensures PPP is a genuine PPP-position reachable under optimal play, the random move injects diversity in the departure P→P′P\to P'P→P′, and the final teacher move provides a correct restoration label for P′P'P′.

Compared to earlier empirical studies of impartial games (Zhou and Riis, 2026, 2023), we “help” the learner in two ways: (i) we represent heap sizes in binary rather than as raw integers, and (ii) we train on perfectly labelled restoration targets (the full set of optimal moves), rather than requiring the agent to infer these targets from sparse win/loss outcomes.

We split the dataset into 80% train / 10% validation / 10% test using a seeded permutation (seed 0), shared by the two representations. The teacher uses the first winning heap; this induces a particular, nonuniform distribution of predecessor positions. The results do not establish invariance to heap permutations, unseen board sizes, or arbitrary self-play histories.

7.2.3 Training and checkpoints

We train each model with supervised learning using cross-entropy to the soft target distribution. We use Adam with learning rate 10−310^{-3}10−3 and batch size 512 for 200 epochs. To study performance as a function of training, we save C=10C=10C=10 checkpoints per model at epochs {1,23,45,67,89,112,134,156,178,200}.\{1,23,45,67,89,112,134,156,178,200\}.{1,23,45,67,89,112,134,156,178,200}.

7.2.4 Evaluation metrics

We evaluate restoration performance on held-out data:

Restoration accuracy (validation/test). Given a held-out example, the saved evaluation takes the argmax over all action logits and counts it as correct if it lies in the support of πopt(⋅∣p′)\pi_{\mathrm{opt}}(\cdot\mid p')πopt​(⋅∣p′). Illegal predictions therefore count as incorrect, and every legal optimal move is accepted. The saved implementation averages batch accuracies equally, including the shorter final batch, rather than weighting them by batch size. The reported decimals are those saved batch means, not exact correct-example counts divided by 100,000. The same convention applies to the displayed validation curve.

7.2.5 Results

One-frame does not learn restoration; two-frame eventually does. Figure 5 shows validation restoration accuracy as a function of epoch. The 1F model has low test restoration accuracy throughout training, approximately 0.075–0.081 across saved checkpoints. We do not identify this range with a measured random-legal-move baseline, which is not supplied in the reported evaluation. In contrast, the 2F model learns the restoration mapping and reaches essentially perfect accuracy with enough training. On the test set (Figure 6), the 2F checkpoints achieve 0.209 at epoch 1, 0.538 at epoch 23, 0.876 at epoch 45, 0.989 at epoch 67, and 0.99998 by epoch 178 (remaining ≥0.99993\ge 0.99993≥0.99993 at epoch 200).

7.3 Single-frame evaluation via FSM-controlled shootouts (multi-head)

Purpose. We complement the two-frame restoration study (Section 7.2) with an experiment targeting the single-frame bypass from Proposition 5.9: learned approximations to the structured rollout policies combined with a finite-state shootout controller (Figure 3). The trained floating-point networks are not claimed to satisfy the formal AC0\AC^0AC0 gate restrictions. The goal is to test the rollout interface itself (how much information can be extracted by controlled shootouts), not to claim that self-play discovers the structured heads without additional inductive bias.

Setup. We consider NIM with N=20N=20N=20 heaps and bit-width k=4k=4k=4 (so B=k=4B=k=4B=k=4 heads), matching the encoding of Section 7.1.1. We evaluate on a balanced test set of 2000 positions with 50%50\%50% PPP-positions (σ=0\sigma=0σ=0) and 50%50\%50% NNN-positions (σ≠0\sigma\neq 0σ=0).

Training the rollout heads. We train a shared-trunk network with B=4B=4B=4 policy heads by imitation learning against the structured policies π0,…,πB−1\pi_0,\dots,\pi_{B-1}π0​,…,πB−1​ from Proposition 5.9. Each head πj\pi_jπj​ subtracts 2j2^j2j from the leftmost heap of size at least 2j2^j2j (falling back to subtracting 1 from the leftmost nonzero heap). When multiple heaps qualify for the same phase of πj\pi_jπj​ (e.g. several heaps have hi≥2jh_i \geq 2^jhi​≥2j), any choice among them produces a rollout with the same total move count and hence the same parity outcome. We therefore train with soft targets: for each position and head jjj, the label is uniform over all equivalent actions, and the loss is cross-entropy against this soft distribution. This avoids penalising the model for an arbitrary tie-breaking choice among equally valid heaps.

Rollout evaluation. Each rollout is deterministic: both players follow the same greedy policy head πj\pi_jπj​ (argmax over legal actions) until termination. The rollout outcome is 1 if the first player wins (makes the last move) and 0 otherwise. Since rollouts are deterministic, a single rollout per (position, head) pair suffices.

The per-head accuracy metric is whether the model’s rollout outcome matches the teacher’s rollout outcome—the correct channel bit—not whether it matches the P/NP/NP/N label directly. Each exact teacher head computes a specified linear functional (r0=σ0r_0=\sigma_0r0​=σ0​; rj=σj⊕σ0r_j=\sigma_j\oplus\sigma_0rj​=σj​⊕σ0​ for j≥1j\ge1j≥1). The learned heads can make channel errors. The FSM uses an OR of the queried outcomes for P/NP/NP/N classification, which is a different task from reconstructing every nim-sum bit.

We make no broader sweep claim without corresponding run records.

8 Discussion and broader implications

The three bypasses identify different resources for handling a global invariant: multi-frame inputs expose local transition information, multiple rollout heads provide complementary channels, and persistent recurrence accumulates the invariant through sequential updates. In the recurrent route, memory connects successive positions while the growing processing horizon supplies the depth needed for parity. The common design principle is to match the information and computation available to the agent to the invariant it must maintain. We briefly discuss directions beyond the specific NIM setting.

Informal interpretation

The three bypasses supply different resources for a global invariant

Motivation, interpretation or scope; not a formal claim.

Explain this How this is formalised

8.1 Theoretical idealisation vs. practical architecture

The simulation theorem concerns Boolean literal-threshold gates with nonnegative weights and bounded thresholds, including their permitted compositions. The experiments use floating-point signed linear layers and ReLU as well as LayerNorm and a Log-Softmax loss. Their difference from the theorem therefore extends beyond normalisation layers. A failure at one finite board size does not establish an asymptotic representational impossibility; success on a finite dataset does not establish strong mastery. The controlled comparison supports a narrower empirical conclusion: the reported transition representation is much easier to learn under this supervised protocol.

Informal interpretation

The experiments' networks differ from the theorem's gates; finite results do not settle asymptotic ones

Motivation, interpretation or scope; not a formal claim.

Explain this How this is formalised

8.2 Local information in combinatorial search

Exposing local invariants may also help guide combinatorial search. Our work on large Condorcet domains used structural constructions and local restrictions (Karpov et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024; Zhou, 2024). This is a motivating analogy, not an AC0\AC^0AC0 reduction or a demonstrated parity lower bound for that search problem. Transferring the present argument requires a precisely encoded computational task.

Informal interpretation

Local restrictions in Condorcet-domain search: a motivating analogy, not a reduction

Motivation, interpretation or scope; not a formal claim.

Explain this How this is formalised

8.3 Beyond NIM: harder impartial games as benchmarks

By Sprague–Grundy theory, every finite impartial game position has a nimber. However, the computational complexity of determining nimbers varies widely. Some impartial games have PSPACE-complete winner problems, such as directed vertex Geography (Schaefer, 1978). Unless P=PSPACE\mathrm P=\mathrm{PSPACE}P=PSPACE, no polynomial-time algorithm solves all such instances. Having a nimber does not supply an efficient way to compute it.

External cited result

Some impartial games (Geography) have PSPACE-complete winner problems

A published result used as background or input; not proved in Lean here.

Explain this How this is formalised

NIM is therefore a diagnostic starting point: its efficient optimal strategy lets us separate a representational obstruction from the difficulty of discovering a strategy. The longer-term benchmark is self-play on impartial games whose strategic structure is only partly understood or whose exact analysis becomes impractical as positions grow. Three candidates illustrate different challenges:

Informal interpretation

NIM is a diagnostic starting point for harder self-play benchmarks

Motivation, interpretation or scope; not a formal claim.

Explain this How this is formalised

  • Sprouts. Players join spots by noncrossing curves, add a spot on each new curve, and keep every spot’s degree at most three. The normal-play outcome conjecture for the standard nnn-spot opening remains open despite substantial progress with exact solvers (Čížek et al., 2026). Learning to exploit the evolving region structure, and to choose winning moves in intermediate positions, would be a stronger test than predicting opening outcomes from nnn alone.

  • Chomp. A move removes a chosen square and all squares above and to its right; taking the distinguished corner loses. Strategy stealing establishes a first-player win on every nontrivial rectangle, but does not supply the winning moves (Berlekamp et al., 2001–2004). Larger boards and their irregular intermediate positions offer a challenge beyond solved special families; the analysis of Chomp continues to pose open problems (Nowakowski, 2025). The benchmark should test move selection and generalisation across shapes, not just the known opening winner.

  • Grundy’s game. A move splits one heap into two nonempty unequal heaps. Whether its nim-value sequence is eventually periodic remains an open problem (Nowakowski, 2025). This offers a test of whether self-play discovers useful structure in component values and how they combine. Testing unseen heap sizes and sums of heaps can distinguish such progress from memorising a finite table.

Informal interpretation

Sprouts, Chomp and Grundy's game offer distinct proposed self-play challenges

Motivation, interpretation or scope; not a formal claim.

Explain this How this is formalised

These are proposed learning challenges, not consequences of the present AC0\AC^0AC0 lower bound. An unresolved structural question is not itself a complexity lower bound, and worst-case hardness need not make a chosen instance distribution difficult. A useful evaluation would reserve unseen sizes and positions, report both training and decision-time computation, and compare play with exact solvers where feasible and strong search baselines elsewhere. Beyond the range of exact verification, improved win rates are evidence of stronger play rather than a solution of an open mathematical problem. The central question is whether self-play discovers reusable strategic structure that extends the range of positions it can handle under a fixed computation budget.

Informal interpretation

Evaluate unseen sizes and positions with explicit computation budgets and solver baselines

Motivation, interpretation or scope; not a formal claim.

Explain this How this is formalised

8.4 What the rollout separation establishes

Theorem 5.12(i) bounds winning-move selection for fixed bit-width, a specified family of root/one-heap measurements and a polynomial-size, constant-depth readout. It does not bound general single-policy search. Within that interface, the BBB structured channels reconstruct the invariant and permit direct move selection. The extra computational resource is the sequential rollout, not the number of neural output coordinates alone. Repeated deterministic measurements of the same affine channel cannot create additional channel bits, but changing the permitted query transformations or controller computation changes the model and can remove that restriction.

Informal interpretation

Theorem 5.12(i) bounds one restricted interface, not general single-policy search

Motivation, interpretation or scope; not a formal claim.

Explain this How this is formalised

8.5 Learning bottlenecks after the representational barrier

The constructions establish that the required computations can be expressed using the stated resources: a shallow restoration rule, structured rollout policies, or a shallow recurrent update iterated over the board. This removes one obstacle before training begins. It does not determine whether gradient descent will find those computations, whether sparse game rewards provide enough guidance, or whether the resulting behaviour generalises.

Informal interpretation

Representability removes one obstacle; it does not determine whether training finds the computation

Motivation, interpretation or scope; not a formal claim.

Explain this How this is formalised

The restoration experiment makes this distinction tangible. Even with transition information and correct supervision, learning passes through an intermediate plateau before reaching near-perfect measured accuracy. The checkpoint diagnostic in Section 7.2 associates the later improvement with the lowest bit of the selected move’s XOR change. We therefore have empirical evidence of a remaining learning bottleneck that is largely overcome in this run, alongside a theorem about a different, representational obstruction. The data do not establish how many distinct learning mechanisms produce the stages or why the transitions occur.

Informal interpretation

Empirical evidence of a remaining learning bottleneck alongside the representational theorem

Motivation, interpretation or scope; not a formal claim.

Explain this How this is formalised

The immediate experimental question is whether AlphaZero-style self-play can discover the restoration rule, complementary rollout policies or recurrent accumulator without their supervised targets. A follow-up should compare outcome-only training with curricula and auxiliary supervision, and examine the learned computations as well as win rates. For recurrence, this includes accurate accumulation and reliable state retention across separators. These controlled NIM tests would establish a basis for the harder benchmarks in Section 8.3; efficient self-play learning and the training regimes needed to achieve it remain open.

Open or deferred item

Whether AlphaZero-style self-play discovers the constructions is open

Explicitly left open, deferred or not yet connected.

Explain this How this is formalised

8.6 Significance and impact

Our results suggest several broader implications.

  • For learning theory: representational sufficiency and learnability are separate questions. A promised predecessor state, complementary measurements, or sequential computation can each alter the resources available for an invariant-based decision.

  • For neural architecture: short history windows (or difference features) can be a principled way to bypass parity-like barriers without scaling depth/width. When history is unavailable, multiple rollout heads offer an alternative within a single-frame architecture. When growing processing time is available, persistent recurrence offers a third route, building the invariant sequentially and retaining it across positions.

  • For practice: circuit complexity can help formulate architectural hypotheses, provided the implemented model satisfies the mathematical assumptions. Tests of those hypotheses should distinguish representation, training dynamics, task distribution and computation budget.

Informal interpretation

Broader implications for learning theory, architecture and practice

Motivation, interpretation or scope; not a formal claim.

Explain this How this is formalised

9 Conclusion

A fixed-depth Boolean literal-threshold model with nonnegative fixed-grid weights and bounded thresholds is simulable in AC0\AC^0AC0. The NIM parity reduction then rules out strong single-frame mastery in that model.

Informal interpretation

Conclusion: AC0 simulation and the single-frame barrier, restated

Motivation, interpretation or scope; not a formal claim.

Explain this How this is formalised

Three constructions identify resources beyond that restricted inference problem. Two-frame access supports constant-depth restoration when the preceding position has nim-sum zero. Distinct structured rollout policies reveal complementary invariant bits; a single-channel limitation holds only under our explicit query and readout restrictions. Persistent recurrence implements running XOR over heap rows, exchanging fixed total latency for a growing sequence of simple updates. Cross-position memory additionally supports comparisons, while replay or board storage supplies the heaps needed for move selection.

Informal interpretation

Conclusion: what the three constructions supply

Motivation, interpretation or scope; not a formal claim.

Explain this How this is formalised

The saved floating-point experiments show a large supervised two-frame restoration advantage and perfect finite-test P/NP/NP/N classification by a learned multi-head controller. The latter coexists with imperfect individual channel recovery. The restoration plateaus and checkpoint diagnostics also show that learning can proceed in stages after transition information is supplied. These observations do not certify the formal gate assumptions, worst-case mastery, or self-play discovery.

Informal interpretation

Conclusion: what the saved experiments do and do not show

Motivation, interpretation or scope; not a formal claim.

Explain this How this is formalised

The contribution is a separation of the information and computation needed for a decision from the training process that must discover it. Establishing when self-play learns the restoration rule, complementary rollout policies or recurrent accumulator remains a distinct experimental question.

Appendix A. Formal definitions of fixed-scale quantised neural models

This appendix provides formal definitions of the fixed-scale quantised neural models used throughout the paper.

A.1 Preliminaries: fixed-scale quantisation and representable parameters

Checked definition or construction

Representable parameters: a fixed finite grid independent of n; negations allowed on wires

Lean contains the definition or construction, with checked properties.

Explain this How this is formalised Lean statement and source

Fix constants W,D∈NW,D\in\NW,D∈N. Define the fixed finite set of representable parameters QW,D={ℓD:ℓ∈{0,1,…,W}}.\Qset_{W,D}=\Big\{\frac{\ell}{D}: \ell\in\{0,1,\dots,W\}\Big\}.QW,D​={Dℓ​:ℓ∈{0,1,…,W}}. In particular, the set of allowable weights/thresholds does not depend on input length nnn. This models fixed-scale quantisation with bounded range: values lie on a fixed grid (step 1/D1/D1/D) and saturate at magnitude W/DW/DW/D, independent of the input length nnn. It is a restricted Boolean gate abstraction; neither floating-point nor general signed fixed-point networks automatically satisfy it. In particular, mere finiteness of a floating-point format is not what drives our AC0\AC^0AC0 containment; the key is that the effective range/scale of thresholds does not grow with fan-in as nnn increases.

We will allow negations on wires (equivalently, AC0\AC^0AC0 has NOT gates). This is standard in circuit complexity and avoids conflating two independent issues: (i) parity hardness vs (ii) monotonicity restrictions.

A.2 Feedforward model

Definition A.1 (Literal-threshold network) A fixed-scale quantised NN\NNNN of depth LLL on nnn Boolean inputs is specified by:

  • Layer widths m0=nm_0=nm0​=n, m1,…,mLm_1,\dots,m_Lm1​,…,mL​, where mℓ≤poly(n)m_\ell\le \poly(n)mℓ​≤poly(n).

  • For each layer ℓ∈{1,…,L}\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}ℓ∈{1,…,L} and unit i∈{1,…,mℓ}i\in\{1,\dots,m_\ell\}i∈{1,…,mℓ​}:

    • weights wℓ,i,j∈QW,Dw_{\ell,i,j}\in \Qset_{W,D}wℓ,i,j​∈QW,D​ for j∈{1,…,mℓ−1}j\in\{1,\dots,m_{\ell-1}\}j∈{1,…,mℓ−1​},

For ℓ≥1\ell\ge 1ℓ≥1, yi(ℓ)  =  H ⁣(∑j=1mℓ−1wℓ,i,j⋅(yj(ℓ−1)⊕ηℓ,i,j)  −  θℓ,i),y^{(\ell)}_i \;=\; \Heav\!\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{m_{\ell-1}} w_{\ell,i,j}\cdot (y^{(\ell-1)}_j \oplus \eta_{\ell,i,j}) \;-\; \theta_{\ell,i}\Big),yi(ℓ)​=H(j=1∑mℓ−1​​wℓ,i,j​⋅(yj(ℓ−1)​⊕ηℓ,i,j​)−θℓ,i​), where H(z)=1\Heav(z)=1H(z)=1 if z≥0z\ge 0z≥0 and H(z)=0\Heav(z)=0H(z)=0 otherwise. A.3 Recurrent model (finite window)

Definition A.2 (Bounded-unrolling recurrence) Fix a time window T∈NT\in\NT∈N. A fixed-scale quantised RNN\RNNRNN consists of:

  • input bits xt∈{0,1}nx_t\in\bits^nxt​∈{0,1}n at time ttt,

  • a hidden state ht∈{0,1}mh_t\in\bits^{m}ht​∈{0,1}m for some m≤poly(n)m\le \poly(n)m≤poly(n),

  • an output ot∈{0,1}ko_t\in\bits^{k}ot​∈{0,1}k for k≤poly(n)k\le \poly(n)k≤poly(n),

  • fixed-scale quantised parameters (weights/thresholds in QW,D\Qset_{W,D}QW,D​ and optional input negations) shared across time,

such that each update ht+1h_{t+1}ht+1​ and oto_tot​ is computed by a depth-LLL fixed-scale quantised threshold network over the current input and earlier states within the window. Each inference starts from an input-independent initial state, and the entire computation producing its output contains at most TTT recurrent updates. No boundary state may carry additional input-dependent computation from before that window. Unrolling this bounded computation yields a feedforward computation of depth O(L⋅T)O(L\cdot T)O(L⋅T). A bound only on the lag between connected states does not imply this bound on total unrolling; the persistent model in Section 5.5 deliberately allows more than TTT updates.

Checked definition or construction

Bounded-unrolling recurrence: at most T updates in total from an input-independent initial state

Lean contains the definition or construction, with checked properties.

Explain this How this is formalised Lean statement and source

A.4 Attention-style model (finite window)

Definition A.3 (Gate-realised attention-style model) Fix a time window T∈NT\in\NT∈N. A fixed-scale quantised LTST\LTSTLTST model processes a sequence (xt−T+1,…,xt)(x_{t-T+1},\dots,x_t)(xt−T+1​,…,xt​) by:

  • computing short-term and long-term attention scores using fixed-scale quantised parameters in QW,D\Qset_{W,D}QW,D​,

  • combining attended summaries through a constant number of layers of fixed-scale quantised threshold computations,

  • producing outputs ot∈{0,1}ko_t\in\bits^kot​∈{0,1}k.

Every score computation, input-dependent coefficient selection, encoding and value aggregation is required to have a polynomial-size, constant-depth implementation in the Boolean literal-threshold gates of Definition A.1. Intermediate state is Boolean, and total unrolling is bounded as in Definition A.2. Under these explicit implementation assumptions, the simulation theorem applies by composition. Merely requiring parameters or coefficients to lie in a finite set is insufficient. This extension makes no claim about standard softmax attention without such a reduction.

Proof of Theorem 2.4. For RNN\RNNRNN and LTST\LTSTLTST with time window TTT, unroll the computation for TTT steps (constant) to obtain a feedforward computation of depth O(LT)O(LT)O(LT) (still constant). Apply the same layer-by-layer replacement.□

Appendix C. Implementation details: shallow circuits and fixed-scale networks

Checked theorem

Shared shallow operations: candidate tests, binary index, recurrent update, threshold realisation

Lean checks a formal statement corresponding to this claim.

Explain this How this is formalised Lean statement and source

The constructions share a small collection of Boolean operations. Each heap is a BBB-bit block, and a move is a validity bit, a binary heap index, and a BBB-bit replacement value. The circuits below have polynomial size in their supplied input length. Their depth does not grow with the number of heaps or bits. All XORs described as shallow here combine two bits, or a fixed number under a bounded-change promise; an XOR of arbitrarily many heap rows is never treated as a primitive gate.

From a game rule to a network. The networks in this appendix are constructed explicitly from the game rules: their connections and weights are specified by an algorithm, rather than found by training. To see what the construction computes, revisit Figure 2. For B=3B=3B=3 and a two-bit index, the output fields are validity 111, index 000000, and value 010010010.

The same move-selection operations are reused when rollout outcomes supply the target nim-sum. In the recurrent construction the target is accumulated over rows, and replay supplies the rows again for candidate testing. These interfaces explain how the constructions avoid asking one shallow network to extract parity from an arbitrary single board. More heaps require more parallel circuitry; executing a rollout or a recurrent scan still requires repeated evaluations.

Each test has size polynomial in BBB. When no cancelling candidate exists, use the first nonzero heap and subtract one. The recurrent update. Scan mode updates the accumulator by two-bit XORs. Replay mode tests the current row against the stored summary, retains the first cancelling candidate and a fallback, and increments the row counter. Counter bit kkk changes exactly when all lower bits are one, so increment also has a shallow circuit. Mode, validity and reset flags select the appropriate register updates. Induction over well-formed token streams proves that every reachable register fits its allotted width and that the output move uses the summary from the same board’s first scan. The input protocol supplies the repeated rows; the controller does not secretly store the board.

Realisation with fixed-scale threshold gates. An OR gate uses weights 111 and threshold 111; a negated literal supplies NOT. Implement AND by De Morgan, as an OR of negated inputs followed by negation. This keeps the threshold bound fixed even when fan-in grows. Constants use no inputs and threshold 000 or 111. Thus all these circuits can use the fixed grid W=D=1W=D=1W=D=1. Identity buffers align layers; every output is proved equal to its source formula on the same finite input. Size counts duplicated formula nodes, and depth counts NOT gates, so these are conservative bounds.

These explicit Lean-checked bounds are not optimised. Together with the polynomial size bounds, they certify the components’ AC0\AC^0AC0 resource requirements. They apply to one evaluation, not to an entire rollout or row scan. The whole-game proofs connect the resulting network outputs to the corresponding game moves and state updates; the time needed to repeat those evaluations remains part of the algorithm.

Where the layer counts come from. For the two-frame selector, the compositional Boolean-depth bound is 4+4+9+3=204+4+9+3=204+4+9+3=20: at most four levels extract the frame difference, four handle candidate tests and replacement bits, nine are allowed by the general selection construction (including fallback and output handling), and three encode the selected heap’s binary index. These are bounds on composed subcircuits, not necessarily the exact number of levels on a shortest implementation. The compiler then gives at most 2⋅20+2=422\cdot20+2=422⋅20+2=42 threshold layers. Similarly, Boolean depths 191919, 171717, 888 and 343434 give the other entries in the table.

The factor of two allows every Boolean level the cost of an AND gate, even though OR and NOT need only one threshold layer. The two additional stages copy inputs into the construction and arrange the output wires; identity gates retain values until they are needed. This uniform construction makes correctness and resource accounting straightforward, but is not a depth optimisation. The table proves that networks within these bounds exist, not that these depths are necessary or that training will discover their weights. A more economical implementation may use fewer layers; establishing sharper bounds would require a separate construction and proof.

Its input also contains the original NBNBNB-bit board, held fixed throughout the decision. This external storage is additional to the state count. The circuit handles head selection, board reload, outcome collection, increment and halt; the depth bound in the table applies to either the early-exit classifier or the all-head schedule.

Appendix D. Weak mastery examples

Example 1 (Pairing strategy) Consider positions (a,a,b,b,c,c,… )(a,a,b,b,c,c,\dots)(a,a,b,b,c,c,…) consisting of pairs of equal heaps. The second player can mirror the first player’s move on the matching heap, maintaining the paired structure until termination, hence winning. The checked binary selector finds the first unequal pair and reduces its larger heap to match its partner. It has constant depth and polynomial size, and wins against every legal opponent from the paired family when playing second. For the first-player role every paired initial board is losing, so weak mastery there would be vacuous.

Checked theorem

Pairing strategy: a constant-depth mirror selector wins as second player on paired boards

Lean checks a formal statement corresponding to this claim.

Explain this How this is formalised Lean statement and source

The distinction from strong mastery is substantive. From the single heap (3)(3)(3), a strategy that takes all three stones wins immediately, irrespective of what it would do elsewhere. It therefore weakly masters that initial position as first player. If it has no prescribed move at (1)(1)(1), however, it fails strong mastery: arbitrary legal play can reach (3)→(2)→(1)(3)\to(2)\to(1)(3)→(2)→(1) with the first player to move. That history is excluded by its own initial action. The general definition and this separation are checked in Lean.

Checked theorem

From (3), taking all stones weakly masters the position but is not strong mastery

This selector gives a winning strategy against every legal opponent response from a nonzero starting position. After the selected move, any opponent move changes one heap by a nonzero XOR difference and therefore makes the nim-sum nonzero again. The selector can restore zero on its next turn. Every legal move strictly decreases the total number of stones, so play terminates; since a nonterminal zero-nim-sum position cannot move directly to the terminal position, the selector makes the last move. The opponent need not follow any rollout policy.
